That depends completely on how you're defining color. Generally we consider your pigmentation to be your color, and pigments work in exactly the opposite manner. White is the absence of any pigment, and black is... well, you can make black with just black pigment, or you can combine cyan, magenta, and yellow to get a brownish approximation of black. CMY doesn't quite work in practice, which is why printers use CMYK.

But then, most black people aren't exactly black, they're a brownish approximation, or considerably lighter than that. So no matter which definition you're using, that's a color.

If you want to argue that we're all colored, I could agree with that.

Yup. Color, when talking about paint or pigmentation, is referring to the colors being reflected, most often by white, or full-spectrum, light. So "white" is an absence of "color" in that it is reflecting the full spectrum of the light hitting it, while "black" represents the presence of all colors of the spectrum of light hitting it, because it is absorbing that spectrum. For white, or full spectrum, light, that means all colors in the traditional visible field, but if you had only a blue light, then anything painted with red pigment would appear "black" in that light, as it absorbs anything not in the red spectrum, which the blue light does not emit.

Being color blind, you have to figure out quickly the difference between pigmentation and emitted light. Understanding comes later... knowing there is a difference is the important bit.

What is the smallest rocket that can escape Earth's gravity?

The escape velocity can be calculated from the Earth's mass, its radius, and Newton's gravitational constant G: v_esc=sqrt(2GM/R) + force due to air resistance .

For the Earth, this speed is 11200 meters per second, about 25,000 miles per hour, or about mach 32.6. Any rocket that can travel equal to or faster than v_esc will leave Earth's gravity.

As far as specific rocket models, I don't know, but there's not many that can reach that with available fuel reserves. However, there have been some recent experiments working on cloaking objects so that energy bends around an object. They've been able to hide objects from photons and other electromagnetic radiation, but I don't know far anyone has come to cloaking areas of space from gravitational energy yet. However, Special Relativity shows that at least electromagnetic energy deflects around gravitational objects so cloaking objects from gravity may be possible in the future.
